# S1. The theory object

The constructs, causal claims, auxiliary assumptions, rival accounts and predictions behind this protocol are held in a single machine-readable file, `theory/intract.theory.yaml`, which is read and checked by the theoryforge package [@bernabeuTheoryforge2026]. Figure 2 of the main text is emitted from that file rather than drawn separately, so the diagram cannot disagree with the hypotheses. Running `theory/build_theory.R` reproduces everything in this section.

The object registers twelve constructs, each with a definition, its intended measurement and its boundary conditions. Eighteen propositions link them, each carrying the mechanism it claims rather than only a direction; fifteen of the eighteen are directed edges of the causal graph, the other three being moderation claims. Six auxiliary assumptions are recorded as first-class entries, five of them corresponding to questions put to the data controller and listed in Table 3 of the main text. Six rival accounts are registered, and seven of the ten predictions are marked diagnostic against one of them.

The rigour checklist scores the object at 90.9 out of 100 with no blocking failure. Every item passes: at least one prediction forbids an observation; the predictions are interval rather than merely directional; mean severity clears the threshold; auxiliary assumptions are fewer than propositions and none was added defensively in response to a prediction; no construct pair exceeds the lexical redundancy screen, whose largest observed similarity is 0.14; every construct carries a definition, a measurement and boundary conditions; the theory's scope is stated; every proposition states a mechanism; at least one relation is causal; at least one prediction discriminates between registered alternatives; a formal-model reference is present, pointing at the design specification used for the precision analysis; and every prediction is reachable from a proposition in the graph.

Because the causal graph is acyclic it yields testable implications, thirty of them. Four are checked as outcome-neutral quality checks in the main text. The most consequential is that the three text properties should be mutually independent once the reading level and the generation route are conditioned on. A first version of the object, lacking the text-provenance construct, implied that they were independent unconditionally, which is false of any real corpus: the same decision about what reading level a text is written for moves lexical, grammatical and discourse properties together. Adding text provenance as a common cause of all three, and giving it an incoming path from the reader's own decoding automaticity, both repaired that implication and derived the adjustment set the analysis uses. Estimating the text coefficients within reading level is therefore a consequence of the theory rather than a precaution added to it.

# S2. Studies from the accompanying systematic review

The Introduction summarises the evidence that motivates the feature set and the moderators. @tbl-computational-reading lists the studies closest to this design in method, meaning a broad set of text features entered into a statistical or machine-learning model to predict a behavioural or comprehension outcome in children.

```{=latex}
\begingroup\small
```

| **Study** | **Sample and design** | **Method and key findings** |
|---|---|---|
| @pickrenContributionTextCharacteristics2022 | Children (*N* = 158, ages 8;8 to 11;2); multilevel logistic models | Word frequency, concreteness, deep cohesion and lexical arousal each predicted passage comprehension after decoding and language comprehension were controlled. |
| @aparicioComprehensionPerformancesExplanatory2022 | Children (*N* = 1,229, grades 2 to 9); multivariate regression | Text and sentence characteristics predicted comprehension, but the direction and size of each effect varied by question type. |
| @ludewigVocabularyTextCoverage2023 | Children (*N* = 924, grade 4); non-linear regression | Estimated lexical text coverage predicted comprehension non-linearly, rising more steeply above roughly 56 per cent coverage. |
| @yuyangniePredictingReadingComprehension2022 | Elementary school students; feature-based prediction model | Sentence complexity, lexical surprisal and rare-word features improved prediction of item-level comprehension scores over a baseline. |
| @wasitokiranaSentenceProcessingIndonesianEnglish2025 | Bilingual children (*N* = 44, 22 with language impairment); eye-tracking | Syntactic complexity impaired comprehension accuracy and slowed recall, disproportionately for children with language impairment. |

| @sortkaerBothSidesStory2021 | Educational app (BookBites); children *N* ≈ 48,000, grades 3 to 6 | App reading time against standardised test scores. Reading speed correlated with ability (*r* = .39 to .48); models predicted 16 to 18 per cent of variance in progress. |

# S3. Language resources for the text features

A multilingual design faces a measurement problem that a monolingual one does not, and it is not solved anywhere in the literature. Concreteness taken from a 40,000-item English rating study, a 350,000-lemma German regression, a 1,400-item Spanish rating study and a 77-language embedding prediction are four different measurements wearing one label. If a resource is chosen language by language on the grounds of local quality, then the method of measurement is perfectly confounded with the language, and standardising within language removes the difference in location and scale but not the difference in construct. There are two clean responses: use one uniformly produced resource everywhere, even where a better native one exists, and accept lower absolute quality for higher comparability; or use native norms and treat every cross-language comparison as descriptive. This protocol takes the first, because language enters the confirmatory models as a grouping factor with varying slopes and those slopes have to mean the same thing in every language. Native norms are then run as a pre-specified sensitivity analysis, and the correlation between the uniform and the native measure is reported for each language in which both exist. That correlation is the quantity that tells a reader how much the choice mattered, and it is reported whether or not it changes a conclusion.

Two consequences of that rule are worth stating plainly, because both revise what an earlier version of this protocol assumed. The `wordfreq` package is not used as the primary frequency source: its data are a frozen snapshot of usage to about 2021, its maintainer discontinued it in September 2024 rather than ingest post-2022 web text contaminated by generated language, and its wordlists for Korean and Greek are built from fewer sources than the rest. The non-English editions of the NRC Valence, Arousal and Dominance lexicon are not used at all: they are machine translations of the English norms made in 2022 rather than ratings collected in the target languages, and their licence is non-commercial.

@tbl-resources gives the primary resource for each feature family, the sensitivity resource, and the coverage across the ten languages the structural sample showed. Where the export turns out to carry more languages, the same rules are applied to them and the table is extended rather than rewritten.

```{=latex}
\begingroup\small
```

| **Feature family** | **Primary, uniform across languages** | **Sensitivity, native where it exists** | **Coverage of the ten sampled languages** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Word frequency | subs2vec, one OpenSubtitles pipeline applied identically to 55 languages [@vanparidonSubs2vecWordEmbeddings2021] | The SUBTLEX family, native and peer-reviewed per language | All ten for the primary. Native norms exist for nine; Korean has none. |
| Age of acquisition | The cross-linguistic norms of Łuniewska and colleagues, an identical 299-word item set rated on an identical scale in 32 languages [@luniewskaRatingsAgeAcquisition2016; @luniewskaCrosslinguisticRatingsAge2019] | Broad native norm sets, which exist at scale for English, Dutch and Polish only | Nine of ten for the anchor set; Korean appears in neither paper. Because 299 words is thin for a text-level mean, age of acquisition is not an anchor for the lexical component and contributes only where a broad native set exists. |
| Surprisal | Goldfish, an identical 125-million-parameter architecture trained on byte-premium-scaled equal-sized data for each language [@chuangGoldfishMonolingualLanguage2026] | mGPT, as a single multilingual model rather than one model per language | All ten at the 1 GB tier. This is the one feature for which a genuinely comparable multilingual resource exists by construction. |
| Word length, lexical density, lexical diversity | Computed from the text directly, so no norm is involved | Not applicable | All ten. |
| Concreteness | Native human ratings only; no value is predicted or projected | Not applicable, since the native norm is the only acceptable measure | Nine of ten, at between roughly 1,400 and 40,000 items [@brysbaertConcretenessRatings402014]. Korean has no indexed equivalent, so concreteness is not computed for Korean and Korean does not contribute to any concreteness analysis. |
| Dependency distance and clause structure | Stanza, whose per-language labelled attachment scores are published and range from 85.5 to 95.2 across these ten [@qiStanzaPythonNatural2020] | UDPipe 2, whose current models track a later Universal Dependencies release and score higher on all ten | All ten in both. Both parsers are run, and the per-language correlation between the two dependency-distance estimates is reported with the feature-pipeline validation. A language in which they disagree materially is flagged and its grammatical component is not used. |
| Adjacent-sentence similarity | BGE-M3, peer-reviewed, over 100 languages, and able to take a whole passage as input [@chenM3EmbeddingMultiLinguality2024] | multilingual-E5-large-instruct, identified by checkpoint rather than by DOI, none being registered | All ten in both. LaBSE is not used: it is optimised for retrieving translation pairs rather than for semantic similarity within a language. |
| Referential overlap, connective density | Computed from the parse and from language-specific connective inventories compiled for this study and deposited with it | Not applicable | All ten, with the inventory for each language checked by a native speaker before use. |
| Valence and arousal | MEmoLon, induced for 91 languages from a single procedure, at roughly two million entries per language [@buechelLearningEvaluatingEmotion2020] | Native rated norms, which exist for nine of the ten | All ten for the primary; Korean has no native norms, so only the primary is available there. |

: Supplementary Table 3. Resources for the text features, the uniform primary and the native sensitivity {#tbl-resources tbl-colwidths="[17,26,22,35]"}

```{=latex}
\endgroup
```

Korean is the weak point and the protocol says so rather than discovering it later. Of the seven norm-based feature families, Korean lacks a subtitle frequency norm, any coverage in the cross-linguistic age-of-acquisition set, any indexed concreteness or imageability norms, and any native valence and arousal norms. What it does have is a uniform frequency estimate, a Goldfish model, both parsers, induced affect and a lexical decision megastudy of 30,930 words. Korean therefore contributes to the lexical and grammatical components and to the affective predictors through the uniform resources, and contributes to no analysis that requires a native norm. A search of Crossref is a poor instrument for Korean-language psycholinguistics, so before the features are frozen a Korean-reading collaborator will search the Korea Citation Index and RISS directly, and any norm set found there will be added to the sensitivity analysis with the addition recorded as a deviation from this protocol. Greek is the next weakest, lacking a large uniform wordlist and a native concreteness set for Standard Modern Greek.

Every tool is recorded by name, version and, where the tool is a model, by the exact checkpoint. Several of the tools named here have no registered DOI, which is normal for research software distributed through model repositories; those are identified by checkpoint rather than cited, and the identifiers are deposited with the feature-extraction code.

# S5. The design analysis in full

The precision analysis simulates the planned crossed structure from the portable design specifications deposited in `design_analysis/`, and is reproduced by `design_analysis/run_design_analysis.R` [@bernabeuPilotr2026]. Full results for every grid point, including the Monte Carlo standard error and Wilson bounds on each decision probability and the counts of converged, singular and warning fits, are in `design_analysis/precision_sweep.csv`. @fig-precision-sup shows the narration and within-child curves that the main text summarises.

![Supplementary Figure 2. Precision for the narration contrast (left) and the within-child accumulated-reading term (right). The narration curve is drawn for a balanced contrast and has to be read against the design effect for the observed narration prevalence, which is given in the main text.](figures/fig_precision_supplement.png){#fig-precision-sup width=100%}

The ordinal outcome behind Hypothesis 5 is handled by a separate script, `design_analysis/run_ordinal_analysis.R`, because a cumulative logit cannot be fitted by the routine the timing models use and treating a three-category rating as continuous would answer a different question. The script keeps the same design specification and the same seed discipline, generates the rating from it, retains each reading with the 30 per cent availability the structural sample showed, applies the protocol's five-rater floor inside every replicate, and fits the model the protocol specifies with `ordinal::clmm`.

The result is the most demanding requirement in the design. At 200, 400, 800 and 1,600 generated texts, with twelve readings each, the 95 per cent interval on a coefficient whose true value is 0.10 log odds has a mean width of 0.44, 0.30, 0.21 and 0.15, and the probability of a determinate verdict never rises above 0.29. The target of 0.90 is therefore not reached within the range simulated, and no crossing is quoted from it. What the grid does establish is the scaling: the fitted exponents of interval width on the number of texts are between -0.51 and -0.53 against a theoretical -0.5, and on that law the requirement projects to roughly 8,000 to 8,700 generated texts, which is about 2,300 to 2,500 texts carrying at least five ratings. Set against the 738 texts the same coefficient needs on reading time, the rating demands an order of magnitude more, which is what a three-category response observed for 30 per cent of readings costs. Both quantities depend on the rating's availability across the full window and on how heavily texts are reused, which the provider-computed counts will supply, and the simulation is re-run at the observed values before any outcome model is fitted. `design_analysis/summarise_ordinal.R` pools the cached grid points and reproduces every number in this paragraph.

# S6. Deriving the priors from the systematic review

Priors for the confirmatory main effects come from the systematic review accompanying this project, through a deterministic pipeline whose rules were frozen before any extraction row existed and which will be run, and its output archived, before any outcome datum is accessed. The mapping from the review's extracted effects to this protocol's coefficients is one-to-many and is fixed as follows. LexicalDifficulty pools the review's word-frequency, lexical-coverage, other-lexical and lexical-diversity effects on reading, sign-harmonised so that frequency and coverage are flipped to a difficulty direction while age of acquisition, word length and surprisal keep their sign. GrammaticalLoad pools syntactic-complexity and sentence-length effects. ReferentialContinuity pools coherence effects, with discourse-structure rows informing the secondary narrativity predictor instead. Valence and arousal pool the text-emotionality rows separately where the extraction distinguishes them.

Estimates are put on a common scale in a fixed order of preference: a standardised beta or a correlation goes through Fisher's *z*; a *d* or *g* converts to *r* using the effective sample size; an odds ratio converts to *d* and then to *r*. Where no effect size is reported but a test statistic is, *r* is recovered from *t* and its degrees of freedom and signed by the reported direction. Unstandardised coefficients without convertible scale information are not pooled and are listed in an exclusion appendix, as are rows whose direction the extraction could not resolve. Pooling is a random-effects meta-analysis within each combination of coefficient and outcome class, with one estimate per paper per relation, so that labelled subgroups of a single paper are never treated as independent. Where a meta-analysis in the corpus subsumes three or more of the corpus's own primary studies, the pooled row is preferred and the overlapping primaries dropped; otherwise the primaries are used and the pooled row dropped, and the alternative is reported as a sensitivity analysis.

The prior is then Student's $t(3, \hat\mu, \sigma)$ with $\hat\mu$ the pooled estimate on the model's scale and $\sigma = 2\sqrt{\mathrm{SE}(\hat\mu)^2 + \hat\tau^2}$, floored at 0.10. The heavy tails let the data override a misplaced centre, and the doubling with a floor guards against the gap between a laboratory comprehension test and a passively timed reading in a game. Interaction terms and any family supported by fewer than two papers keep the generic weakly informative priors. The complete prior table, the forest plots, the conversion arithmetic and the list of excluded rows will accompany the Stage 2 report, and the pipeline's output is timestamped and deposited before the extract is transferred.

# S7. Data-access certification

The text below was sent to the data controller on 7 August 2026 and is reproduced as it stands. The bracketed fields are completed and the document signed before this protocol is submitted; if any of them is still open at submission, that is stated here rather than left to be inferred.

> Gameloft confirms that, as of [date]:
>
> 1. An export of *Let's Story* reading sessions was built on [build date], covering [window] and comprising [n] rows, in the file or files listed in the accompanying record with their SHA-256 checksums.
> 2. That extract is held by Gameloft and has not been transferred, in whole or in part, to the University of Oxford research team or to anyone acting for it.
> 3. It will be transferred only on written confirmation of in-principle acceptance.
> 4. Material shared with the team to date: a 35-row sample and the data dictionary, shared on 27 July 2026 to confirm the structure of the table; the story texts; and the counts and file record described above.
> 5. No analysis relating story text to reading time has been conducted by Gameloft or reported to the team.
>
> Owner: [name, role]  
> Deputy: [name, role]  
> Signed: [name, role, date]

Two points about clause 4. The 35-row sample carries real reading times, and the main text discloses it rather than relying on this clause to do so. The story texts are named here because the editorial office confirmed in advance that stimulus materials may be received before submission, and because every linguistic measure in this protocol is computed on them; they contain no behavioural outcome.

The accompanying record referred to in clause 1 is the manifest: the column list, the row count, the cut-off timestamp, the build date and a SHA-256 checksum for every file. It is deposited with this protocol. Any row removed from the held extract between the build and the transfer, whether by an erasure request or otherwise, is recorded by the data controller and reported at Stage 2 with its effect on the counts.
